passage: Sonali: can I ask you something about Ritesh in 9B Mridul: the one who threw his chair on Monday? Sonali: yes. today he went totally silent when I moved his seat. then exploded over a missing pen Mridul: I'd have sent him out honestly Sonali: I nearly did. then I remembered the training. I asked him after class, "what happened?" instead of "what's wrong with you?" Mridul: and? Sonali: he said a lot has happened at home. he didn't give details. I didn't push Sonali: I'm keeping his seat the same and telling him before any change. and no calling him out in front of the class Mridul: makes sense Sonali: I've also told the safeguarding lead and referred him to the school counsellor, both today Mridul: good. I'll try the same in my class

qa.q: What did Ritesh explode over after going silent?
qa.a: A missing pen.

qa.q: Why did Sonali ask 'what happened?' instead of 'what's wrong with you?'
qa.a: Sonali felt concerned rather than angry, and wanted to understand Ritesh rather than blame him, remembering the training.

qa.q: Which steps did Sonali take after talking to Ritesh?
qa.a: Keeping his seat the same, warning him before changes, not calling him out publicly, and passing it to the safeguarding lead and the counsellor the same day.

qa.q: What might it be like for Ritesh to be asked "what happened?" and to be told before his seat changes?
qa.a: Ritesh may feel less judged and safer, since he is not blamed and nothing changes around him without warning.

grounding: A teacher sees a student who goes silent or explodes over small things, asks what happened rather than what is wrong, keeps routines predictable, avoids public shaming and refers him to a counsellor.

passage: In the small-town government school, Gurleen Ma'am noticed that Anjali, fourteen, had changed since the winter. Some days she said nothing at all, eyes on the window. Other days she blew up over nothing. When Gurleen rearranged the benches, Anjali shouted, "Why does everything have to change?" and burst into tears. The class turned to stare. Gurleen didn't scold her in front of them. She said calmly, "Anjali, come help me with the charts," and took her to the staffroom. There she asked, "What happened, Anjali? You don't have to tell me everything." Anjali said only, "Things at home got scary." Gurleen didn't push. The next day Anjali's bench was back in its old place, and Gurleen wrote the week's timetable on the board every Monday. She also spoke to the school counsellor and the safeguarding lead that same afternoon.

qa.q: What did Gurleen Ma'am rearrange that upset Anjali?
qa.a: The benches.

qa.q: What does Anjali's outburst 'Why does everything have to change?' suggest?
qa.a: It suggests that change felt frightening to her, perhaps because things at home had become scary.

qa.q: Which of Gurleen Ma'am's choices were most helpful?
qa.a: Taking Anjali aside instead of scolding her publicly, asking what happened, keeping routines predictable and speaking to the counsellor and safeguarding lead the same day.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Anjali if Gurleen Ma'am had scolded her in front of the class?
qa.a: Anjali would likely have felt more ashamed and less safe, with the whole class staring and seeing her as a troublemaker.

grounding: A teacher sees a student who goes silent or explodes over small things, asks what happened, keeps a predictable routine, avoids public shaming and refers her to a counsellor.

passage: In his classroom in Nairobi, Ivan saw Wanjiru, fourteen, explode when a boy scraped his chair loudly behind her. She swept her books off the desk and shouted. Last week she had gone silent for a whole lesson after a door slammed. Ivan didn't send her out or scold her in front of everyone. After class, he asked quietly, "Something happened that made that noise hard. Do you want to tell me what happened?" She stared at the floor. "There was a crash near our house. I still hear it." He nodded. "Thank you for telling me." He kept the same seating and lesson order every day and let her sit near the front, away from scraping chairs. That afternoon he referred her to the school counsellor.

qa.q: What made Wanjiru explode in class?
qa.a: A boy scraped his chair loudly behind her.

qa.q: How did Ivan feel when Wanjiru shouted and threw her books?
qa.a: He seemed calm and concerned rather than angry, choosing not to scold her in front of everyone.

qa.q: What did Ivan do that helped?
qa.a: He asked what happened instead of what was wrong, avoided public shaming, kept a predictable routine and referred her to the counsellor.

qa.q: How might Wanjiru have felt when Ivan asked what happened?
qa.a: She may have felt relieved and understood, able to share the real reason for her reaction.

grounding: Shows a teacher seeing a student explode or go silent over small things, asking what happened, keeping routines predictable, avoiding shaming and referring to a counsellor.

passage: In the Class 10 room, a boy shouted a joke across the room, and Mahima, fifteen, went completely still. Her pen stopped. Her eyes went blank. Gopika Ma'am noticed it was the third time that week, always after sudden loud voices. She didn't call on Mahima or ask, "What's wrong with you?" in front of the class. She finished the lesson calmly and asked Mahima to help carry books to the staff room. There she asked softly, "When things get loud, you seem to go far away. Has something happened?" Mahima nodded without speaking. Gopika said, "You don't have to tell me now. We keep the same routine here every day, and the counsellor is someone good to talk to." She walked Mahima to the counsellor's office that same period.

qa.q: Where did Gopika Ma'am ask Mahima to help carry books?
qa.a: To the staff room.

qa.q: How did Gopika Ma'am feel seeing Mahima go still for the third time?
qa.a: She was concerned and attentive, noticing a pattern after sudden loud voices.

qa.q: What made Gopika Ma'am's response supportive?
qa.a: She avoided public questions, asked privately what had happened, promised a steady routine and walked Mahima to the counsellor.

qa.q: How might Mahima feel when told she doesn't have to tell now?
qa.a: She may feel relieved and safer, not pushed to share before she is ready.

grounding: Shows a teacher seeing a student go silent over small triggers, asking what happened privately, keeping routines predictable and referring to a counsellor.

passage:
Dear Zeenat,
I'm writing to refer Rafiq from Class 9 to you. Over the past month I've seen a pattern. When anyone raises their voice, even laughing, he either flares up and shouts, or goes silent and puts his head down for the rest of the lesson. Last Tuesday he threw his bag after a desk fell over.
I've stopped asking him "What's wrong?" in front of others. Instead, after class I asked, "What happened?" He told me there was a fire at his uncle's shop in the summer and he was inside when it started.
I've kept the seating and lesson order the same every day, and warned him before any noisy activity. No public discipline.
Could you see him this week? He has agreed.
Uma

qa.q: What did Rafiq do last Tuesday?
qa.a: He threw his bag after a desk fell over.

qa.q: How does Uma feel about Rafiq's behaviour?
qa.a: Uma seems concerned and understanding, seeing a pattern linked to fear rather than simply bad behaviour.

qa.q: Which of Uma's steps help Rafiq?
qa.a: Asking what happened in private, keeping routines predictable, warning before noisy activities, avoiding public discipline and referring him to the counsellor.

qa.q: How might Rafiq feel being warned before noisy activities?
qa.a: He may feel safer and more in control, less likely to be startled into flaring up.

grounding: Shows a teacher seeing a student explode or go silent over small things, asking what happened, keeping routines predictable and referring to a counsellor.

passage:
I'm Nilesh, the students call me Nilesh Sir, and I teach Class 9 maths. Let me tell you about Saurabh.
Last year he'd explode over tiny things. A dropped pen, a changed seat. Other days he'd go silent and stare. The old me would have said, "What's wrong with you?" in front of the whole class.
Instead, one day after class, I asked, "What happened this year, Saurabh?" Not what's wrong. What happened. He was quiet, then said his family lost their home in the monsoon flood. They were living in a relief camp for a while.
So I changed some things. Same seat every day. I write the plan on the board each morning, no surprises. I never corrected him in front of others. And I referred him to our counsellor, with his parents' agreement.
He still has bad days. But he stays in the room now.

qa.q: What happened to Saurabh's family's home?
qa.a: They lost their home in the monsoon flood.

qa.q: How did Nilesh Sir feel when Saurabh first exploded over small things?
qa.a: He felt puzzled and tempted to snap back, but he chose curiosity and concern instead.

qa.q: Which of Nilesh Sir's changes helped Saurabh, and why?
qa.a: Asking what happened, a fixed seat, a daily written plan, no public correction and a counsellor referral made class predictable and safe.

qa.q: What is it like for Saurabh when his seat is suddenly changed?
qa.a: It probably feels alarming and unsafe, bringing back the upheaval of losing his home.

grounding: Nilesh Sir sees a student explode or go silent over small things, asks what happened, sets predictable routines, avoids public shaming and refers him to a counsellor.
